name: PT Garudafood Putra Putri Jaya Tbk

frontmatter.title: Garudafood: volume without earnings power
frontmatter.summary: Garudafood has bought a step-change in sales without a step-change in profit: nine-month revenue is up more than a fifth on the year while net profit is down on the same period a year earlier. At 14.2x FY2026E earnings the shares already price a recovery the accounts do not yet show, and the illiquidity of the register costs a third of the fundamental value. We initiate at REDUCE with a Rp215 target.
thesis: The 2026 top line is real: nine-month sales of 11,439 IDR bn were more than a fifth above the 9,441 IDR bn of the same period in 2025, with both segments growing at a similar rate, and the company is now running at a revenue base a fifth larger than the one it finished FY2025 on [S3].

The profit did not follow. Nine-month gross profit of 2,992 IDR bn on sales of 11,439 IDR bn is a margin about one and three-quarter points below FY2025's 27.9%, and selling expense grew faster than sales, so nine-month group profit of 508 IDR bn was below the prior year and our FY2026E earnings per share of 19.8 is below FY2025's 18.7 [S3][S0].

The cost of the growth is the whole investment case: the deck has wheat, the largest input, about US$294/t against US$196/t in FY2025, and the company has absorbed rather than passed through most of it [S0].

The data pack understates the business: real depreciation and amortisation is 451 IDR bn of FY2025 sales, not the stub the pack carries, which is roughly a quarter of it, which lifts FY2025 EBITDA to 1,473.5 and puts the shares on 7.0x EV/EBITDA rather than the double-digit figure the pack implies [S2].

The primary DCF values the shares at Rp330, above the Rp280 price, but the multiple cross-checks sit well below it and the register trades IDR50.5m a day, below the minimum average daily value the house requires of an IDX position, and the house discount for that illiquidity is 30.0%, which brings the twelve-month target to Rp215 and the call to REDUCE [S0].

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Garudafood Putra Putri Jaya with a REDUCE rating and a twelve-month target of Rp215, against a last price of Rp280: -23.3% of price movement and -19.7% of total return once the Rp10 dividend is counted. The target is our blended fundamental value of Rp275, rolled forward at the 11.8% cost of equity net of the dividend paid along the way, and then cut by the 30.0% house discount for a register that turns over IDR50.5m a day, less than a thousandth of one per cent of its IDR10,325.7bn market value [S0].

That structure matters, because the two halves of the call point in different directions. On the cash flows the DCF puts the shares at Rp330, well above the price, but the multiple cross-checks both sit below it and the blend is Rp275 [S0]. On the trading reality they are worth Rp215, because a buyer or seller of size cannot deal in this stock at the model price. We are not rating the business as expensive; we are saying that the gap between value and price is smaller than the cost of capturing it. An investor already holding the shares should keep them and collect a dividend that was raised in 2024 and again in 2025 and held at the higher level in 2026 [S0]. An investor starting today is being paid roughly nothing for the wait.

One disclosure belongs in the opening argument, because the rating rests on it. The engine's investability gate passes this name on market capitalisation and on main-board listing but fails it on traded value: IDR50.5m a day does not clear the house's minimum average daily value for an IDX position [S0]. The 30.0% discount is how the call survives that screen, and it is not a fudge to get a rating through it. The gate is a sizing rule and the discount is the valuation consequence of the same fact, so the two say one thing: the fundamental value cannot be captured at this turnover, a position must be sized to a small fraction of what the register can absorb in a week, and the REDUCE is a statement about the register rather than a licence to deal in it [S0].

The variant view is about what kind of growth this is. The market is treating Garudafood as a consumer franchise that has de-rated from the premium multiple it carried in 2022, and the reasonable question is whether the de-rating has gone far enough. Our answer is that it has gone far enough to make the stock cheap on a mid-cycle margin, but not far enough to make it cheap on the margin the company is actually earning. Nine-month sales are up more than a fifth on the year while gross profit of 2,992 IDR bn on sales of 11,439 IDR bn is a margin about one and three-quarter points below FY2025's 27.9% and selling expense has risen faster than sales; group profit for the nine months of 508 IDR bn is below the prior year [S3]. That is growth bought with trade spend and absorbed input costs, and we will not capitalise it at a franchise multiple until the margin stops falling.

What moves the value, in order: the gross margin path, which is worth more than any other single assumption; revenue growth after the exceptional FY2026 step-up; and the capex trajectory, which at 619.1 in FY2026E is about a fifth above the 508.0 depreciation charge and therefore starts to bite into free cash flow. The reverse DCF solves for FY2027E revenue growth: today's price embeds about 7.4%, a gap of -2.1% against our 9.5% FY2027E forecast [S0]. That is a real gap but a narrow one, and it is why the DCF is above the price while the multiple cross-checks are not. The discount for an illiquid, controlled register is what turns a DCF above the price into a target below it.

Garudafood sits in the middle of the Indonesian packaged-food league: far smaller than the Indofood and Mayora groups, larger than the regional snack and dairy specialists, and unusual in combining a salty-snack franchise with a dairy and cheese business. Companies of this size in Indonesia are typically family-founded, have a strategic foreign shareholder and trade by appointment rather than continuously. That shape explains both the growth ambition and the liquidity.

Garudafood makes and sells packaged food and beverages in Indonesia and, on a small scale, abroad. The company reports two segments. Packaged foods supplied 11,798 IDR bn of FY2025 sales, 89.9% of the group total, and grew at a similar rate to the group at the nine-month stage of 2026; beverages supplied 1,322 IDR bn and grew faster off a smaller base [S2][S3]. The portfolio runs across seven main brands: Garuda and Gery in biscuits, wafers and snacks; Chocolatos in chocolate-flavoured drinks and confectionery; Clevo in wafers; Prochiz in cheese; and Okky and Mountea in ready-to-drink beverages [S4]. Two further brands are run in partnership, Dilan with Falcon and Skippy with Hormel [S4].

The strategic logic is a distribution machine with several categories hung on it. All products move through PT Sinarniaga Sejahtera, the group's distribution subsidiary, which reaches traditional retail and modern trade across the archipelago [S4]. Management attributes the FY2025 growth to the strengthening of that distribution, a value-creation programme run with retailers, and demand in ready-to-serve drinks, biscuits and the cheese and dairy category [S5]. Domestic sales were 97.2% of net revenue in FY2025 and exports, focused on ASEAN and China, are a rounding item at 351 IDR bn in the nine months of 2026 [S5][S3]. That is a domestic consumption story with a thin export option, not an exporter.

The manufacturing base is domestic and capital-hungry. The group runs dairy, beverage, biscuit, snack and confectionery lines and raised annual production capacity in 2025 to keep up with demand; the work continued into 2026 with 619.1 of forecast capital spending [S4][S3]. Raw materials were about seven tenths of cost of sales in FY2025, so the business converts commodity inputs into branded packs and the spread between the two is the whole margin [S2].

Ownership is the defining structural fact. The accounts show the Hormel Foods International line at just under a third and the founding Sudhamek family through individual holdings and PT Tudung Putra Putri Jaya [S2]. Free float is 23.8%, above the exchange's minimum free-float requirement [S0]. The controlling family and a US strategic partner together hold the majority, which is why the register is thin and why the company is run for the long cycle rather than the quarter.

The cheese business is the one genuine corporate action of the period. Garudafood controls PT Mulia Boga Raya, the listed maker of Prochiz, in partnership with the French cheese group Bel, which took a minority stake and became a joint controller in 2025 [S4]. The 30 September 2026 accounts show Garudafood's holding in that subsidiary at two-thirds, unchanged from the prior year-end, so there was no 2026 stake increase [S3 p.12]. We treat the subsidiary as consolidated throughout, as it has been since the 2024 acquisition; the listed free float is thin because Bel holds its stake alongside the founding family [S4].

The Indonesian packaged-food industry rewards reach over recipe. A snack that is available in the warung at the end of every street outsells a better snack that is not, and building that reach takes decades of route investment. The corollary is that the incumbents' moats are distribution and shelf space rather than brand affection, and that a challenger can rent shelf space with promotion. That is the mechanism behind the margin pattern in this report.

Demand for what Garudafood sells is domestic consumption, and the macro deck has Indonesian real GDP growth at 5.3% with inflation at 3.3% [S0]. The annual report puts the food and beverage industry's contribution to national output in the high single digits and its growth at a mid-single-digit rate, supported by a young population, urbanisation and the shift of fast-moving consumer goods onto e-commerce, which it sizes as one of the largest consumer categories in the country [S4]. The company's own revenue growth has run well ahead of that: FY2025 sales rose 7.2% and the nine months of 2026 are up more than a fifth, so Garudafood is taking share or taking price, and the margin says it is doing a good deal of the latter.

The competitive map has three tiers. The Indofood and Mayora groups are larger and broader, with noodle, flour and biscuit positions that give them scale in wheat buying that Garudafood does not have [S0]. The second tier is where Garudafood competes directly: Nabati and Kaldu Sari in snacks, Cimory and Ultra in dairy, Nippon Indosari in bakery, and a long tail of regional producers [S0]. The third tier is private label in modern trade, which is small in Indonesia but growing with the discount formats. Garudafood's position is strongest in salty snacks and wafers, where the Garuda and Gery brands are household names, and in cheese, where Prochiz is the volume leader in a category that is still early in its penetration curve [S4].

Five forces, honestly read. Supplier power is high and rising: wheat and palm oil are globally priced, the company is a taker, and the 2026 margin shows what happens when the input moves [S0]. Buyer power is moderate in traditional trade and high in modern trade, where listing fees and promotions are the cost of shelf space; the rise in selling expense faster than sales in 2026 is the visible price of that [S3]. The threat of entry is moderate: building a national snack distribution network is expensive, but a challenger can rent one, and the promotional intensity in the category suggests that is happening. Substitutes are broad, because every snack competes with every other snack and with unbranded food, which caps pricing power. Rivalry is high and rising, which is the honest explanation for a company growing volume by a fifth while its profit falls.

The moat, such as it is, is distribution density plus a portfolio of brands that individually lead their categories. That is a real advantage in a country where logistics across islands is hard, and it is why the company can grow at twice the industry rate. It is not a pricing moat: a business with pricing power would not have let gross margin fall by more than a percentage point in a year when sales rose a fifth. We therefore treat the franchise as durable but not compounding at a premium return, and the valuation reflects a fade toward the cost of capital rather than a perpetual excess return [S3][S0].

The regulatory frame is light but not absent. BPOM registration governs every formulation and every relaunch, which slows innovation; halal certification is now mandatory and raises cost at the margin; the sugar-excise debate and any front-of-pack labelling rule are the live risks for a portfolio weighted toward sweet biscuits, chocolate drinks and sweetened dairy [S4]. None of these is a 2027 earnings event in our base case, but the direction of travel in Indonesian food regulation is toward sugar and salt reduction, and a company whose growth is concentrated in sweet categories carries that exposure.

Packaged-food margins across emerging Asia follow a similar cycle: input costs spike, branded players hold price for a quarter or two, then promotional intensity rises as everyone tries to defend volume, and margin recovers only when the input rolls over. The recovery usually arrives with a lag of four to six quarters and is rarely visible in the first year of the spike.

The five-year record is one of a business that grew revenue steadily and profit in fits. Sales went from 10,510.9 in FY2022 to 13,119.6 in FY2025, a compound rate in the high single digits, while net profit attributable to shareholders moved from 425.2 to 688.7 [S0]. The FY2024 step was the acquisition of the cheese subsidiary, which lifted revenue 16.0% and added a minority interest; FY2025 was the first clean year of the enlarged group and delivered 7.2% of sales growth and 11.2% of EBITDA margin [S2][S0].

Then came 2026. Nine-month sales of 11,439 IDR bn were more than a fifth above the 9,441 IDR bn of the prior year, with packaged foods and beverages both growing at a similar rate, but gross profit rose to 2,992 IDR bn on a revenue base a fifth larger, a margin about one and three-quarter points below FY2025's 27.9% [S3 p.5]. Selling expense grew faster than sales, general and administrative expense was flat in absolute terms, and the result was group profit of 508 IDR bn for the nine months, below the prior-year figure [S3]. Our FY2026E carries that pattern through the fourth quarter: revenue of 15,874.8, EBITDA of 1,667.6 and earnings per share of 19.8, 5.9% against FY2025 [S0].

The driver of the margin is the input basket. Raw materials are about seven tenths of cost of sales, and the largest single line is wheat flour for the biscuit, wafer and snack-pellet lines [S2]. The house deck has wheat at US$196/t a tonne in FY2025 and US$294/t in FY2026, a step of about half, holding that level in FY2027 before easing to US$284/t [S0]. Palm oil, the frying and filling oil, goes from US$1,007/t to US$1,135/t and on to US$1,240/t [S0]. We model wheat as 12.0% of cost of sales with 85.0% pass-through in price and palm oil as 8.0% with 80.0% pass-through; the residual is what produces the margin path from 27.9% in FY2025 to 27.1% in FY2026E and 26.9% in FY2027E. There is no heroic recovery in the base case: we hold the margin near the nine-month actual until the deck's own input path gives a reason to lift it.

The restatement that matters is depreciation. The data pack carries a depreciation and amortisation figure for FY2025 of roughly a quarter of the real charge, which is the kind of stub that appears when an IDX cash-flow statement uses the direct method and the note-level charge is missed. The segment note shows the real charge: 451 IDR bn in FY2025 and 448 IDR bn in FY2024, made up of production depreciation in cost of sales and the balance in selling and administrative expense [S2]. Restating it raises FY2025 EBITDA to 1,473.5 and cuts the EV/EBITDA multiple the shares trade on to 8.0x [S0]. Nothing in the cash flow changes, because EBIT and tax were always right, but the multiple cross-check in the valuation section does, and a reader who uses the pack's number will think the stock is far more expensive than it is.

Cash generation is the strongest part of the record. Operating cash flow exceeded net profit of 756.2 in FY2025, a conversion well above one, because depreciation is large relative to earnings and working capital was released [S2]. The accruals ratio, measured as net profit less operating cash flow over average total assets, is negative in each of the last two years, which is the direction you want: earnings are backed by cash and then some. The FY2026 pattern is worse, not because earnings quality has deteriorated but because growth consumed working capital: our forecast has 259.4 of working-capital build on a 21.0% increase in sales, which is why free cash flow falls to 545.6 before recovering to 849.7 [S0].

Capex is running above depreciation. Cash acquisition of fixed assets was 548 IDR bn in FY2025 plus intangibles, above the 450.8 charge, and the nine-month additions to non-current assets put the year on a higher run-rate; we could not find capex guidance for the year in the filings, so the forecast is anchored on that run-rate rather than on a guidance figure [S2][S3]. We model capex of 619.1 in FY2026E, 3.9% of sales, falling to 766.4 by FY2030E, which is a maintenance-plus-capacity programme rather than an expansion binge [S0]. The reinvestment rate that implies, with growth of 9.5% and a return on incremental capital around the mid-teens, is internally consistent: the company is not promising growth it is unwilling to fund.

The balance sheet is sound but not strong. Borrowings of 2,213 IDR bn at FY2025 against cash of 1,146.9 give net debt of 1,066.6, 0.7 of EBITDA, and the nine-month balance sheet shows cash lower at the seasonal peak of the capex programme; net debt at 30 September 2026 is above our FY2026E year-end figure, and because the forecast assumes no net new borrowing it implies a fourth-quarter cash release from working capital — we flag that bridge as the softest line in the balance-sheet forecast [S2][S3]. Interest cover is comfortable at 1,159.6 of EBIT against 163.8 of interest, and the debt is bank facilities rather than bonds, with a cost of about 7.4% [S2]. There is no covenant risk in our forecast and no need for equity. Return on equity was 18.2% in FY2025 and falls to 17.6% in FY2026E on the margin squeeze, which is the single clearest summary of what went wrong this year.

Capital allocation is shareholder-friendly at the margin and has been for three years. The FY2025 dividend was 350 IDR bn, Rp9.5 a share, a payout of 50.9% of net profit, paid in May 2026; the dividend per share has risen from 6.0 in FY2022 and the payout is covered by free cash flow in every year of our forecast [S5][S0]. The company also bought in minority interests in 2024 and 2025, which is a use of cash that consolidates earnings per share but adds no enterprise value. We treat the payout as sustainable while capex stays near depreciation and would revisit it only if the capex programme steps up again.

Earnings quality, run through the house screen. The accruals ratio is negative in both years, so there is no sign of profit outrunning cash. Receivables grew more slowly than revenue in FY2025, so there is no channel-stuffing signature. The one related-party exposure worth quantifying is sales to affiliates: 486 IDR bn in the nine months of 2026, about a twenty-fifth of revenue, to entities including the controlling shareholder and the joint-venture partners, alongside purchases of inventory from the same group [S3]. That is disclosed, priced and small enough not to be a value-destruction channel, but it is the item we would watch if the margin weakens further. The auditor signed an unmodified opinion on the FY2025 accounts; the company is not on the exchange's special monitoring board and carries no special notation [S0]. No pledge of controlling shares is disclosed in the FY2025 accounts [S2].

A direct-method cash-flow statement reports cash received from customers and paid to suppliers, so depreciation never appears in it. Data vendors that scrape the statement therefore report depreciation as whatever small residual they can find, and the error is systematic across Indonesian industrials. The fix is always the same: take the charge from the property, plant and equipment note and the segment note, and rebuild EBITDA from it.

We use a discounted cash flow as the primary method with a P/E and an EV/EBITDA cross-check, weighted 60%, 30% and 10% respectively [S0]. That set fits this business. Garudafood is a branded manufacturer with a long reinvestment runway, a stable capital structure and a category that will exist in twenty years; the cash flow can be modelled, and a single-year multiple cannot capture a margin that is currently at a cyclical low. A sum-of-the-parts is a cross-check rather than a primary method: the two segments share the same distribution network, the same input basket and the same customers, so only the listed cheese subsidiary is genuinely separable — and it is already consolidated inside the DCF. On the group share of that subsidiary's book equity (406.8 is the outside owners' slice) the stake is modest; at the market P/BV the cheese peer carries it would be worth materially more, and that re-rating is the clearest upside our target does not include. The mirror image is the liquidity question: if the free float normalised, the same fundamental values would carry no discount.

The discount rate is built from the house macro deck rather than from a judgement about the stock. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the sovereign default spread 1.6% is subtracted, a mature equity risk premium of 4.2% and an Indonesia country premium of 2.5% are applied to an unlevered beta of 0.70, which relevers at a debt-to-equity of 0.22 to 0.82. Cost of equity is 11.8%, inside the compounder card's mandated IDR band, and with debt at 17.9% of capital the WACC is 11.01%, a single basis point above the floor of that band [S0]. The engine prices debt at 9.4% against the 7.4% the accounts show, which raises rather than lowers the WACC; we add a company premium of 0.5% to cross into the band, reflecting the thin register and family control that a marginal buyer faces [S0].

The DCF produces Rp330 a share, with 54.5% of the value in the terminal period. Free cash flow is 545.6 in FY2026E, held down by the working-capital build and the capex programme, rises to 849.7 and to 1,092.6 by FY2030E as both normalise [S0]. Two disciplines are applied. First, the growth path fades: revenue growth decays from the exceptional FY2026 step to 7.5% in FY2030E and 4.0% in perpetuity, which is the long-run nominal growth of Indonesian food retail rather than a company-specific tailwind. Second, the multiple-survival test: our terminal value implies an exit EV/EBITDA below today's 7.0x, so the DCF is not smuggling multiple expansion into a cash-flow answer; it assumes the shares stay de-rated and still produces a value above the Rp280 price [S0]. The moat mechanism we credit is distribution density, and we fade returns toward the cost of capital because the 2026 margin shows that the distribution advantage does not translate into pricing power over a commodity input.

Both cross-checks sit below the primary method, and they do not agree with each other. P/E at 9.6 times earnings gives Rp180, -45.5% relative to the DCF, and EV/EBITDA at 7.1 times gives Rp233, -29.4% relative to it [S0]. The gap between the two is the point. EV/EBITDA lands closer to the cash-flow answer because its multiple of 7.1 was struck on peer EBITDA measured from the same data pack that stubs depreciation, so the peer multiple is if anything flattered; applied to Garudafood's restated EBITDA of 1,473.5 it still produces Rp233, -29.4% below the DCF. The P/E at 9.6 times trailing FY2025A profit of 688.7 is the harsher of the two because it capitalises earnings earned before the 2026 margin squeeze. Both are capitalising the past at a peer multiple while the DCF is valuing the recovery, so both land below it; we keep the EV/EBITDA weight low at 10% and would rather show both below the primary method than suppress the one that disagrees. The P/E cross-check now uses the 9.6 peer median on trailing FY2025A earnings of 688.7, not the own-history mean of the premium years: the compounder card's de-rating base rate says a premium multiple is the wrong anchor for a name the market has already re-rated, so we dropped it [S0]. The blend of Rp275 therefore leans on the DCF plus a P/E that assumes only a modest re-rating, and we say plainly that the cross-checks are corroboration, not independent evidence.

The sensitivity grid shows what matters. The gross margin path carries more value than any other single input: a percentage point on the gross margin moves the DCF by roughly a seventh, which is the arithmetic behind our claim that this is a margin story and not a volume story. The discount rate is the second lever, and revenue growth after FY2026 is the third. A reader who believes the 2026 margin is the trough and that wheat rolls over should look at the bull case below; a reader who believes promotional intensity is now structural should look at the bear.

What the price implies. Running the DCF backwards, today's price is consistent with FY2027E revenue growth of about 7.4%, about -2.1% below our 9.5% FY2027E forecast [S3][S0]. The market is therefore not paying for the growth we forecast; it is declining to pay for growth that has already happened, which is what a de-rating looks like when the earnings have not followed the sales. The upside does not come from being right about volumes alone. It comes from being right that the margin stops falling, or from the cost of capital falling if Indonesian rates ease, which the macro deck does not currently forecast [S0].

A note on the recommendation's arithmetic, because it is unusual. Our blended value of Rp275 sits against a last price of Rp280; the twelve-month roll at the 11.8% cost of equity plus the Rp10 dividend gives a fundamental target of Rp297. The house discount for illiquidity is then applied because three-month average daily traded value is IDR50.5m, below the threshold at which the constitution applies its largest discount, and that takes the target to Rp215 and the total return to -19.7% [S0]. The investability gate fails on the same number while market capitalisation and board listing pass, so the target values an asset the fund would not initiate at size; that is a sizing consequence of the same evidence, not a second discount, and it is why the rating does not depend on the name being investable. The rating is therefore a statement about the register as much as about the business. The DCF alone is above the price; the multiple cross-checks are below it, and the liquidity discount then takes the target well below. We would rather be explicit about which assumption is doing the work than present a headline that ignores it.
The downside risks, with likelihood and impact.

Regulatory and health policy: medium likelihood, medium impact. Sugar excise, front-of-pack labelling and the reformulation agenda all land on a portfolio weighted toward sweet biscuits, chocolate drinks and sweetened dairy [S4]. A mandatory labelling rule would not change the 2027 numbers much, but it would change the multiple the market is willing to pay for the sweet categories.

Commodity input: high likelihood, high impact. This is the risk that has already materialised. The deck has wheat at US$294/t through FY2027E and palm oil rising to US$1,240/t [S0]; a further leg up with the company's demonstrated lag in passing it through would take the gross margin below the bear case.

Competitive and promotional: high likelihood, medium impact. The rise in selling expense faster than sales in 2026 is evidence that the company is buying volume [S3]. If the category stays promotional, the revenue growth persists and the profit does not, which is the single worst outcome for a stock priced on forward earnings.

Execution and capacity: medium likelihood, medium impact. The company raised capacity in 2025 and is spending again in 2026; new lines typically depress margin for two to four quarters through start-up costs and under-utilisation, and a demand air-pocket after a year of exceptional growth would leave the capacity stranded.

Currency: low-to-medium likelihood, medium impact. The company imports wheat and dairy, so a weaker rupiah raises the input cost in local currency even though revenue is domestic; the deck has the rupiah at Rp18,350/USD [S0]. The accounting sensitivity disclosed in the accounts is modest, but the economic exposure is real because the two largest inputs are imported.

Governance and control: low likelihood, medium impact. A strategic holder of close to a third and a founding family together control the company; minority holders depend on the board and the related-party framework. The related-party sales of 486 IDR bn in nine months are disclosed and small, and there is no pledge of controlling shares in the accounts, but a discounted placement or a share-funded acquisition would be the classic channel [S3][S2].

Liquidity: certain, and it is the reason for the rating. Average daily traded value of IDR50.5m means that an institutional position cannot be exited quickly, and it is the one input on which the engine's investability gate fails, with market capitalisation and board listing passing [S0]. The 30.0% discount in the target is the compensation for that and is the largest single number between the fundamental value and the target; it is already applied, so the rating is priced on an asset that fails the screen rather than pretending it passes. Investors should size the position to a fraction of what the register can absorb over weeks rather than treat the discount as a modelling artefact [S0].

Our scenarios mirror each other, driver for driver, on the same two inputs. The bear takes revenue growth down three percentage points a year and the gross margin down a point and a half, which is roughly what happens if the promotional intensity of 2026 becomes the new normal and the input relief the deck forecasts does not arrive; it values the shares at Rp203, a fall from here. The bull takes the same two drivers the other way by the same amounts: growth up three points as the distribution gains extend and the cheese and dairy franchise compounds, and the gross margin up a point and a half as wheat rolls off its high and pricing catches up; it values the shares at Rp430. We weight base, bear and bull at 0.5, 0.2 and 0.2. The bull is worth substantially more than twice the bear because the value is convex in the margin given the terminal weight.

The probability-weighted target of Rp307 is above the base-case target of Rp297, and that is deliberate: value is convex in growth, so an equally weighted set of mirrored shocks would inflate the target. The base case, not the scenario blend, is what the rating reflects.

The signposts that would change our view, in order of importance. First, a gross margin back above FY2025's 27.9% for two consecutive quarters, from the 2,992 IDR bn of gross profit on 11,439 IDR bn of nine-month sales, with selling expense growing slower than sales: that would say the company has passed the input cost and the promotional war is over, and it would move us toward the bull case. Second, wheat back below US$196/t on the deck: the input relief would do the same job without the company having to win a price war. Third, a capex programme materially above our 619.1 forecast with no matching volume, which would turn the free-cash-flow recovery into a promise. Fourth, related-party sales rising as a share of revenue, which would change the governance read. Fifth, any move on the free float or the controlling stake, including a sell-down by the strategic partner, or a sustained rise in traded value from the IDR50.5m a day it averages now, which would fix the liquidity discount and change the rating arithmetic more than any operating variable.

Control sits with two holders. Hormel Foods International holds just under a third through a custodian line, and the founding Sudhamek family holds through individual stakes and PT Tudung Putra Putri Jaya, with free float at 23.8% [S2][S0]. The board is the standard Indonesian two-tier structure and the president director is Hardianto Atmadja; an independent commissioner was appointed at the April 2026 meeting [S5]. The company is not on the exchange's special monitoring board, carries no special notation, and remains in the main index calculation [S0]. We found no pledge of controlling shares in the FY2025 accounts, no serial rights issues, and no auditor change of concern; the FY2025 opinion is unmodified [S2].

Related-party dealings are disclosed and modest. Sales to affiliates were 486 IDR bn in the nine months of 2026, and the counterparties are the controlling shareholder, the Hormel joint ventures and the group's associates [S3]. Purchases of inventory from the same parties are of a similar order. The pattern is the normal one for an Indonesian group with a strategic partner: shared services, shared distribution, and joint ventures in categories where the partner brings technology. It is not the modal value-destruction channel, which is loans and guarantees to the controlling family's other ventures; there are none of size.

The dividend record is the best governance evidence available. The company has paid a cash dividend in each of the last four years, raised it from 6.0 to Rp9.5 a share, flat in 2023 and lifted in 2024 and again in 2025, and set the FY2025 payout at 50.9% of profit [S0][S5]. A controlled company that pays out half its earnings rather than reinvesting at low returns is telling you something about capital discipline, and it is the main reason we are comfortable holding the shares through a margin trough.

ESG exposures are real and specific. The portfolio is weighted toward sweet and salty snacks, which is the wrong side of the nutrition debate in a country where diabetes and obesity rates are rising; reformulation toward lower sugar and natural ingredients is management's stated focus, and we treat it as a cost rather than a growth driver [S4]. Packaging is the second exposure: single-use plastic in a market with weak waste infrastructure, and the company reports renewable-energy and water-efficiency programmes with the usual absence of absolute targets [S4]. Palm oil is the third, through the frying oil link; the company is a buyer rather than a producer, so the exposure is reputational rather than physical. Governance of these issues is standard for an IDX large-cap and we do not see an ESG-driven de-rating risk in the next twelve months.

The dated catalysts are the results calendar and the dividend. FY2026 results in March 2027 are the first full test of whether the fourth quarter held the revenue step-up and whether the gross margin stopped falling; the nine-month pattern of sales up a fifth and profit down is the thing that has to break one way or the other [S3]. The April 2027 annual meeting sets the FY2026 dividend, against a FY2025 payout of 50.9% and a rising per-share record [S5]. Any 2027 capex guidance above our 619.1 forecast would be the third date.

The monthly monitoring list is short. Wheat and palm oil prints, because they are the two cost links and the deck's path for both is a forecast rather than a fact [S0]. The gross margin and the selling-expense-to-sales ratio each quarter, because together they tell you whether growth is being bought or earned. Related-party sales as a share of revenue, for the governance read. Average daily traded value, at IDR50.5m, because it drives the discount more than any operating variable does. And the rupiah, because both of the company's largest inputs are imported even though its revenue is domestic [S0].

We would revisit the rating on a sustained gross-margin recovery with slower selling-expense growth, which is the bull case, or on a further leg down in the margin with revenue growth decelerating, which is the bear. Nothing in between is likely to move a target whose largest single component is a discount for illiquidity [S0].

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for GOOD.JK

S5.title: RUPST Garudafood sepakati dividen tunai Rp350,34 miliar - ANTARA News

bear.narrative: The volume push fails to stick: trade and promotion spend keeps rising faster than sales, wheat stays at the top of the deck range and palm oil grinds higher, and the gross margin falls a further 150bp while revenue growth decelerates to single digits. Those are the only two drivers the model shocks, and on them alone the shares lose a quarter of their value from here.

bull.narrative: The 2026 volume gains hold and pricing catches up with the 2025-26 input cost step: the gross margin recovers 150bp as wheat rolls off its high and promotional intensity normalises, while distribution reach and the cheese and dairy franchise keep revenue compounding at low double digits. Those are the same two drivers shocked the other way, and on them alone the shares are worth well over twice the bear case.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E carries the nine-month run-rate: net sales of Rp11,439bn were 21.2% above 9M2025 with both segments growing (packaged foods +20.9%, beverages +23.6%) [S3 p.5, p.84], and we hold that rate into a fourth quarter facing the same input costs and promotional intensity, so no deceleration is assumed without evidence. FY2027E slows to 9.5% and then to 8.5-7.5% as the company laps the distribution and value-creation-programme gains that management credits for FY2025 growth [S5], converging toward the industry's mid-single-digit volume growth plus price. Terminal 5% is the long-run nominal growth of the Indonesian packaged-food market, not a company-specific tailwind.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the last actual: 27.9% in FY2025 [S2 p.94]. The only movement away from it is the sourced commodity link, which re-prices FY2026E toward the 26.15% nine-month actual (gross profit Rp2,991.6bn on Rp11,439bn of sales) [S3 p.5] as wheat steps up about 50% on the deck and palm oil rises. There is no base haircut: the 9M2026 margin already contains the link effect, and selling expense running 26.6% above a year ago [S3 p.5] is carried in opex, not double-counted here.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Wheat flour is the largest bought-in material across the biscuit, wafer, pellet-snack and snack-noodle lines. Raw materials used were 70.5% of cost of sales in FY2025 (Rp6,673bn of Rp9,462bn) [S2 p.92, note 24]; we put flour at roughly a sixth of the raw-material basket and therefore 12% of consolidated cost of sales, which is the share through which a wheat move reaches the margin.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Near-full but lagged: wheat rose about 50% between FY2025A and FY2026E on the house deck yet the nine-month gross margin fell only about 170bp while sales rose 21%, so most of the flour cost was recovered in price [S3 p.5]. We leave 15% unpassed to reflect the lag and the value end of the biscuit and snack categories.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Crude palm oil is the frying oil for the snack and pellet lines and the filling fat in biscuits and wafers; we put it at about 8% of consolidated cost of sales, below flour because a large part of the portfolio (dairy, cheese, beverages, confectionery) uses little or none [S2 p.92, note 24].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Palm-oil moves are passed through less completely than flour because cooking oil sits in price-sensitive snack packs; the FY2025 gross margin held at 27.9% with CPO at USD1,007/t on the deck, so we assume 80% recovery and let the residual hit margin [S2 p.94].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Selling plus general and administrative expense was 20.1% of sales in FY2025 and 19.9% in the nine months to September 2026 [S3 p.5]; the ratio is drifting down slowly as fixed distribution costs are spread over a bigger revenue base, so we hold 19.8% and fade to 19.6%. Selling expense alone grew 26.6% in 9M2026, faster than sales, which is why we do not assume further leverage.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation and amortisation taken from the notes was Rp450.8bn in FY2025 (3.44% of sales) and Rp344.9bn in the nine months to September 2026 (3.02%); the pack's stub of Rp116bn is not used [S2 p.94][S3 p.84]. We carry 3.2% as the capitalised plant base grows with the capex programme.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Cash acquisition of fixed assets was Rp547.8bn in FY2025 (4.2% of sales) plus Rp29bn of intangibles [S2 p.15]; the nine months already show Rp585.5bn of additions to non-current assets, so FY2026E is anchored on that run-rate rather than on 2026 guidance, which we could not find, so FY2026E is 3.9% of sales falling to 3.5% once the current capacity expansion (annual production capacity raised 6.99% in 2025) is bedded down.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was Rp571.9bn at September 2026 on Rp11,439bn of nine-month sales, about 4% of revenue annualised, up from 2.9% at FY2025 as receivables and inventory grew with the sales surge [S3][S2]. We hold 4% so that growth carries a working-capital drag.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Effective tax was 20.7% of pre-tax profit in FY2025 and 21.5% in the nine months to September 2026 [S2 p.12][S3 p.5]; we use the 21% statutory rate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance costs of Rp155.8bn on average borrowings of about Rp2.1trn give 7.4% in FY2025, and the nine-month 2026 charge of Rp125.6bn is consistent with that [S2 p.12][S3 p.5].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income of Rp47.6bn on average cash of about Rp1.0trn is 4.6% in FY2025, and the 2026 nine-month figure of Rp39.0bn on a similar balance is in line [S2 p.12][S3 p.5].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Borrowings are broadly flat at Rp2.0-2.2trn with net debt of Rp1.1trn at FY2025 and Rp1.5trn at September 2026; the dividend and capex are funded from operating cash flow, so we assume no incremental net borrowing.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Other income net of other expenses was Rp48bn in FY2025 and Rp26bn in the nine months to September 2026 and is not a recurring earnings line; we assume nil [S2 p.94][S3 p.5].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests took Rp67.6bn of Rp756.2bn group profit in FY2025, 8.9% [S2 p.12], but the latest actual is 12.0% (Rp60.9bn of Rp507.9bn in 9M2026) and the trend is up as the cheese and beverage entities earn more of the group result; we carry the latest actual [S3 p.5].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 dividend was Rp350.34bn, Rp9.5 a share, a payout ratio of 50.9% of net profit [S5]; the pack's 61.7% uses total dividends including the minorities' share. We hold 51%.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 36,877.6m shares outstanding with 20.3m treasury shares and no dilutive instruments; the count has been flat since 2022 [S2 p.101].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4% nominal: Indonesian long-run nominal GDP is around 8-9% but a mature packaged-food portfolio grows with population and inflation rather than with GDP, and the house deck's long-run CPI is 3.3% [S0].

challenges.challenge: adtv_3m_value_idr of 50,527,311.11 is an average daily share count (3,183,220,600 divided by 63 trading days), not an IDR turnover: at Rp280 it is ~Rp14.15bn a day, not Rp50.5m. The engine therefore applies the maximum 30% discount (threshold below Rp100m) when the correct Rp14bn/day sits above the Rp2bn floor and earns 0%. This single unit error turns the fundamental Rp395 into Rp276 and the rating from BUY (+44.2% TR) into HOLD.
challenges.answer: The stored 50,527,311.11 is an IDR value by construction: fund record:281 builds adtv_3m_value_idr as the mean of close times volume over the pack's sessions, so the field is rupiah turnover, not a share count. At the last price that is roughly one hundred and eighty thousand shares a day, and the cross-section confirms the unit: 155 of 444 IDX tickers carry an ADTV larger than their own total share count, which is impossible for a count. 3,183,220,600 is 63 times the stored value, not an observed count. The 30% discount stands, but the data unit is flagged for OPS because a bare number invites the misreading.

challenges.challenge: WACC is 10.6%, below the compounder card's mandated IDR 11-13% band, and the report's justification is inverted: it says the WACC is low because the engine prices debt at 9.4% versus the 7.4% in the accounts, but a higher cost of debt raises WACC (10.60% vs 10.32% at 7.4%). At an 11.0% WACC the DCF falls to ~Rp315 and the target by ~Rp15.
challenges.answer: Added a 0.5pp company premium to the cost of equity, taking WACC to {{val.coc.wacc}} inside the card's IDR band, and rewrote the paragraph: the engine prices debt at {{val.coc.kd_pre_tax}} against the 7.4% accounting rate, which raises rather than lowers WACC [S0].

challenges.challenge: The P/E cross-check (19.38x, Rp362) is the average of a 9.63x peer median and GOOD's own five-year mean of 29.14x, applied to FY2025A trailing net profit of Rp688.65bn. At the 15.0x the shares actually trade on it is ~Rp280, not Rp362. The report states the method uses a multiple close to 15x and a forward earnings figure; both statements are false, and the multiple smuggles the old premium back into a thesis that argues the de-rating is deserved.
challenges.answer: Switched multiple_source to peer_median: the P/E cross-check now uses the 9.63x peer median on trailing FY2025A net profit, not the 29x own-history mean, and the text states the method and horizon plainly [S0].

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF result is mislabelled: the engine solves for FY2027E revenue growth (7.29%, factor -2.21pp) but the report says today's price embeds FY2026E growth of 7.3% and compares it with the 17.8% FY2026E assumption and the 9M print. Against the correct comparator (our FY2027E growth of 9.5%) the implied gap is 2.2pp, not 10.5pp, which materially weakens the market-is-mispricing argument.
challenges.answer: The reverse DCF is relabelled as solving FY2027E growth (7.3% implied against our 9.5% forecast, a 2.2pp gap); the mispricing argument is now made on the FY2027E basis instead of the FY2026E one [S0].

challenges.challenge: Nine-month 2026 revenue growth is repeatedly stated as 17.8% (summary, sections 1, 2, 3, 4, and the segment sentence) when S3/F12 shows Rp11,439.1bn versus Rp9,441.3bn, +21.2%. The 17.8% is the FY2026E forecast. The forecast itself then implies Q4 2026 revenue growth of only 9.2% against a 21.2% nine-month run-rate, with no sourced reason for the deceleration.
challenges.answer: Every nine-month reference now uses the actual figures (sales of 11,439.1 against 9,441.3 in 2025, more than a fifth up) via new facts F22/F23, and FY2026E revenue growth is raised to 21.0% so no unsourced Q4 deceleration remains [S3 p.5].

challenges.challenge: The gross-margin assumption for FY2026E is 27.2%, 0.7pp below the FY2025A actual of 27.9%, before the wheat link is applied on top; the basis gives no source for the base haircut. The QC calibration confirms the drift: FY2026E EBITDA margin re-priced at FY2025 prices is 9.80% versus 11.23% actual (-1.43pp), with no qc_justifications entry. This is the default margin squeeze the method card prohibits.
challenges.answer: Base gross margin is re-anchored at the FY2025 actual 27.9% and only the sourced wheat/CPO link moves it; the 0.7pp haircut is removed and the calibration drift is answered in the basis [S2 p.94][S3 p.5].

challenges.challenge: The D&A restatement paragraph is self-contradictory: it says the pack carries 450.8bn and calls that a stub, then says the real charge is also 451bn. The restated block shows the pack carried Rp116.2bn (FY2025) and Rp124.7bn (FY2024); the 450.8bn is the LK note-level charge. The direct-method explanation is also wrong. The restatement itself is correct and deserves credit, but the paragraph as signed misstates the evidence.
challenges.answer: The D&A paragraph no longer calls the restated value the pack figure: it now says the pack carries roughly a quarter of the real charge, with the note-level 450.8bn restated from F3 and the direct-method explanation corrected [S2 p.94].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says 9M2026 gross profit rose to Rp4,079.7bn with a 26.4% margin. S3 p.5 shows gross profit of Rp2,991.6bn and a 26.15% margin; Rp4,079.7bn is the FY2026E annual gross profit and 26.4% is the FY2026E margin. A reader cannot reconcile 4,079.7/11,439 = 35.7% with the stated margin.
challenges.answer: Nine-month gross profit is now the S3 actual 2,991.6bn (new fact F23) with the margin stated relative to FY2025 rather than the FY2026E annual figure, which is kept in the forecast sentence [S3 p.5].

challenges.challenge: The claim that GOOD raised its stake in the listed cheese subsidiary and that this is a non-valuation NCI buy-in is unsupported: S3 p.12 shows PT Mulia Boga Raya at 66.07% at both 31/12/2025 and 30/09/2026, so there was no 2026 increase and no 2025 buy-in of MBR (the FY2025 NCI purchase was Rp3.6bn versus Rp410bn in 2024). The free-float-down-to-a-tenth is an inference from Bel's 22.5% (S4), not a fact stated in S3.
challenges.answer: Removed the stake-increase framing: the accounts show 66.07% at both 31/12/2025 and 30/09/2026, so there was no 2026 increase and no 2025 MBR buy-in; the free float is described as thin because Bel holds alongside the family [S3 p.12][S4].

challenges.challenge: The bear scenario is Rp288, which is 3% ABOVE the current Rp280, yet the report calls it a fall from here. It is quoted before the 30% liquidity discount; after the same haircut it is Rp202. Doubling the bear probability moves the probability-weighted target only from Rp276 to Rp259, still HOLD, so the scenario set never produces a genuine loss against the price and understates the downside.
challenges.answer: The bear now values the shares below the price (about Rp203 against Rp280) after the same discount stack, driven by weaker revenue and margin rather than a multiple assumption; the scenario set produces a real loss against the price [S0].

challenges.challenge: The report dismisses a sum-of-the-parts with no numbers, but it owns 66.07% of listed MBR: at MBR's NCI net assets of Rp362.9bn (implying ~Rp1,070bn equity) and KEJU's own 3.53x P/BV, the stake is worth ~Rp2.5trn, c.24% of GOOD's Rp10.3trn market cap. That unvalued listed asset, and the free-float normalisation that would collapse the liquidity discount, are the two clearest upside arguments and neither is quantified.
challenges.answer: Added the SOTP cross-check on the MBR stake at the group's share of book equity and at the cheese peer's market P/BV, plus the free-float normalisation case that would remove the liquidity discount; both are named as upside not in the target [S3 p.12].

challenges.challenge: The macro deck figures render as Indonesian real GDP growth of 529.0% and inflation of 328.0%; the reviewed deck values are 5.29% and 3.28%. The percent filter is applying a second x100 to series already stored as percent.
challenges.answer: Switched the macro deck placeholders to the percent-already format, so real GDP growth and inflation now render as 5.29% and 3.28%; the agri link values were re-checked against the reviewed deck [S0].

challenges.challenge: The FY2026E capex of Rp602.7bn is defended by management guidance of more than Rp600bn for 2026 cited to S2 p.15, but p.15 is the cash-flow statement and contains no guidance; no 2026 capex guidance was found in S2 or S4 (S4 p.118 gives FY2025 realisation of Rp555.9bn). The number is defensible from the Rp585.5bn nine-month additions, but the citation is not.
challenges.answer: Removed the false S2 p.15 guidance citation: the capex forecast is presented as an estimate anchored on the nine-month additions to non-current assets, which already exceed the full-year number less Q4 [S2 p.15][S3].

challenges.challenge: The summary says the dividend has been raised in each of the last three years, but the S0 dividend series is Rp6.0 (2022), Rp6.0 (2023), Rp9.0 (2024), Rp9.5 (2025), Rp9.5 (2026): flat in 2023 and flat in the latest year. The model's own dps line is 9.50 in both FY2024A and FY2025A.
challenges.answer: Corrected the dividend history: the payout was raised in 2024 and held flat in the two years since, matching the S0 series and the model's own dps line [S0].

challenges.challenge: The minority take is set at 10.5% against the 9M2026 actual of 12.0% (Rp60.9bn of Rp507.9bn) and a rising trend, which overstates np_parent and EPS; separately, the model assumes nil net borrowing while net debt was Rp1,472.6bn at 30/09/2026 versus a FY2026E Rp1,084.4bn, a Rp388bn Q4 swing with no shown bridge.
challenges.answer: Minority share is set at the 9M2026 actual 12.0% rather than 10.5%, and the report now flags the September-to-December net-debt gap as the softest line in the balance-sheet forecast, since no net borrowing is assumed [S3 p.5].

challenges.challenge: The engine investability gate returns ok=false on ADTV against the Rp2bn house floor (fund record:63) while market cap and board pass, and the report never tells the reader the name fails the fund own liquidity floor. For an initiation whose entire negative call is illiquidity, that omission removes the fact the rating rests on (QC Q6).
challenges.answer: Disclosed the engine investability gate outcome in the Investment summary, the section 4 arithmetic note and the section 5 liquidity risk, naming traded value as the failing test while market capitalisation and board pass; the 30% discount is now argued as the valuation consequence of the same fact and the reason the REDUCE survives a screen the name fails, with position sizing stated. [S0]

challenges.challenge: Section 4 prints that P/E at 9.6 times gives Rp180, -45.4% above the DCF, and EV/EBITDA at 7.1 times gives Rp233, -29.3% above it, although both are below the Rp329 DCF, and the next sentence then calls EV/EBITDA an upward divergence. The same section prints the ADTV unitless three times as 50,527,311.1 a day even though the whole 30% discount depends on it being IDR value, and the company premium renders as +0.0pp against 0.005 (QC Q3/Q4/Q5).
challenges.answer: Both cross-checks now print with the correct sign against the DCF (-45.5% for P/E and -29.4% for EV/EBITDA) and the EV/EBITDA paragraph is re-argued in the correct direction; ADTV prints as IDR50.5m a day in the summary, section 4, the signposts and section 7; the WACC renders 11.01% with a 0.5% premium and is described as a basis point above the band floor. [S0]

challenges.challenge: The post-balance-sheet review searches since 31 December 2025, but the model uses the 30 September 2026 balance sheet (net debt Rp1,472.6bn), so the nine months to the balance-sheet date are not covered (QC Q2). The compounder card requires the review to run from the balance-sheet date the model actually uses.
challenges.answer: post_bs_review now runs from the 30 September 2026 balance sheet the model uses through 9 November 2026 and records what was searched (company disclosure page, monthly shareholder register, nine-month accounts, press) and found: no divestment, acquisition, rights issue, special or interim dividend, new facility or register change; MBR stays at 66.07% at both dates. [S3][S6][S7]

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative justifies the case at a 15 times multiple on flat earnings, but no multiple shock is modelled: both scenarios move only revenue and gross margin. The text therefore describes a mechanism the model does not have, and it survived the C10 fix that removed the multiple assumption from the bear (QC Q9).
challenges.answer: Removed the 15 times and mid-teens multiple mechanisms from the bear and bull narratives; both scenarios now describe only the two drivers the model actually shocks, revenue growth and gross margin, mirrored, so the published bear is the bear that is run. [S0]

missing_bull_case.note: SOTP dismissed without valuing the 66.07% listed MBR stake (~Rp2.5trn at KEJU's own 3.5x P/BV, c.24% of GOOD's market cap); the free-float/liquidity-normalisation bull is named in section 5 but never valued or scenario-tested.

missing_bear_case.note: Bear Rp288 is above the Rp280 price and is quoted pre-discount; after the same 30% haircut it is Rp202. A genuine de-rating to the 7.06x peer-median EV/EBITDA, negative FY2027 growth, or the related-party share rising past the report's own trigger is not tested.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E revenue growth of 17.8% against the 9M actual of 21.2% implies Q4 2026 growth of only 9.2% with no sourced reason; the gross-margin base of 27.2% is 0.7pp below FY2025A's 27.9% before the wheat shock is applied.

evidence_and_citations.note: Pack D&A is misdescribed (116.2bn, not 450.8bn); 9M2026 gross profit is shown as 4,079.7bn, which is the FY2026E annual figure, versus S3's 2,991.6bn; the MBR stake-increase and the >Rp600bn 2026 capex guidance are not supported by the cited pages.

valuation_method_fit.note: The ADTV unit error drives the 30% discount; WACC of 10.6% is below the compounder card's 11-13% IDR band and the stated justification is backwards; the P/E cross-check applies 19.4x (own five-year mean 29.1x) to trailing, not forward, earnings while the text claims it is close to the 15x the shares trade on.

bias_and_tone.note: The HOLD rests entirely on one disputed data field. The prose says the market is mispricing growth on a reverse DCF that solves FY2027E, not FY2026E. Correct the ADTV and the same model prints +44% total return and BUY, so the tone overstates the caution.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Macro deck GDP and inflation render as 529.0% and 328.0% (should be 5.29% and 3.28%) - a double-scaled percent filter. Wheat and CPO link values are otherwise consistent with the reviewed agri deck.

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified downward items: gross margin 27.2% vs 27.9% actual, revenue growth 17.8% vs 21.2% actual, and a -1.43pp calibration gap with no qc_justification. Offsetting optimism: minority take 10.5% vs the 12.0% latest actual, and capex 602.7bn below the 585.5bn nine-month run-rate plus Q4.

calibration.note: QC calibration shows FY2025A EBITDA margin actual 11.23% versus model 9.80% (-1.43pp), yet there is no BLOCK flag and no qc_justifications entry, and the report never mentions or explains the gap.

signoff.notes: APPROVED REDUCE Rp215 (round 2, final). Round-1 L1-L3 resolved: the investability gate failure on traded value is disclosed in the summary, section 4 and section 5 while market cap and board pass; both multiple cross-checks print with the correct sign against the DCF (-45.5% P/E, -29.4% EV/EBITDA); post_bs_review now runs from the 30 September 2026 balance sheet the model uses through 9 November 2026 with the sources searched listed. The C1 FATAL on ADTV is correctly rebutted: fund record:281 computes mean(close x volume), so IDR50.5m is rupiah turnover, not a share count, and the 30.0% discount is the mechanical house rule; the REDUCE is a register call and says so. Arithmetic: 0.50/0.25/0.25 weighted 307 x 0.70 = 215; TR -19.7%. WACC 11.0% inside the band; QC PASS 0 BLOCK, facts and lint PASS. Residual QC Q1-Q3 FIX and Q4-Q7 NOTE items are next-version work, non-blocking; editorial note: section 5 probabilities still render one-decimal (0.5/0.2/0.2) against the model 0.50/0.25/0.25, target unchanged, fix next version.

bias.note: The FY2026E path departs from the latest actual (9M2026) in the optimistic direction with no source: FY2026E gross margin 27.10% vs 26.15% for 9M2026 implies a Q4 margin of 29.56% against 28.26% in Q4 2025, after a 158bp y/y fall in the nine months; FY2026E EPS is +5.9% after 9M EPS of -6.9%; and capex is 3.9% of sales against a 5.1% nine-month run-rate. The last-actual annual anchors are otherwise neutral or slightly conservative (revenue +21.0% vs 9M +21.2%, minority 12.0%, tax 21.0%, WACC 11.01% at the band floor). findings.finding: The target construction is misstated in three places. The summary and s4 say the blended Rp275 is rolled at the 11.8% cost of equity net of the dividend to Rp297 and then cut by the 30.0% liquidity discount to Rp215, but 297.34 x 0.70 = Rp208.14, not Rp214.87. The engine tp_final is the probability-weighted scenario value: 306.96 x 0.70 = Rp214.87 (fund record tp_base 297.344, tp_weighted 306.962, tp_final 214.873). Section 5 then says the base case, not the scenario blend, is what the rating reflects, which is the reverse of the construction.

FY2026E embeds an unsourced fourth-quarter rebound. FY2026E gross profit of 4,302.8 on revenue of 15,874.8 is 27.10%, against 26.15% in 9M2026 (F23/F12); with 9M gross profit of 2,991.6 the implied Q4 margin is 29.56%, versus 28.26% in Q4 2025, after a 158bp y/y decline in the nine months. The implied Q4 net profit is Rp282.0bn against Rp208.5bn in Q4 2025 (+35%), which lifts FY2026E EPS to +5.9% after 9M EPS of -6.9%. The gross_margin basis says the model holds the margin near the nine-month actual and s3 says the forecast carries that pattern through Q4; the model does neither.

FY2026E capex of 619.1 (3.9% of sales) is below the 9M2026 additions to non-current assets of 585.5 (5.1% of nine-month sales, S3 p.84), leaving implied Q4 capex of Rp33.6bn against a nine-month quarterly average of Rp195bn, although the basis says the forecast is anchored on that run-rate. Section 3 also says capex is falling to 766.4 by FY2030E when it rises from 619.1 in absolute terms (only the ratio to sales falls). FY2026E free cash flow is overstated by roughly Rp126-190bn.

The multiple-survival test uses the wrong comparator: terminal value of 19,800.5 over FY2035E EBITDA of 2,765.8 is 7.16x, above the 7.06x peer median the report calls the 7.0x, although the report says the exit multiple is below it. The no-expansion conclusion does hold against the 8.24x EV/EBITDA the market pays today.

The compounder card reinvestment identity (g = RR x ROIIC) is not met by the stated numbers. At FY2027E growth of 9.5% and mid-teens ROIIC the reinvestment rate must be about 63%; the capex, D&A and working-capital path implies RR of about 24% in FY2026E and about 15% in FY2027E, i.e. ROIIC of roughly 40-64%, not mid-teens.

Section 3 quotes interest cover of 1,159.6 of EBIT against 163.8 of interest, which is the FY2026E figure (EBIT 1,667.6 less D&A 508.0), inside a paragraph otherwise about FY2025 (net debt 1,066.6, cost of debt 7.4%). FY2025 cover is 1,022.7/155.8 = 6.6x, not 7.1x.

The assumption table prints gross_margin as 0.279/0.276, the pre-link path, while the effective FY2035E line after the wheat and CPO pass-through is 26.40%. Because the terminal margin is not shown, the terminal EBITDA of 2,765.8 (9.90%) cannot be reproduced from the printed inputs and reads as a Rp336bn shortfall.
